Why Frame Material Matters More Than You Think

Your license plate lives in one of the harshest environments on your car. It faces direct rain, road salt in winter, UV exposure all summer, and high-speed vibration every time you drive. A cheap metal frame may look fine on day one, but after six months of real-world use, the picture changes dramatically.

Silicone frames solve problems that most drivers don't realize they have until they go to sell their car and find a rust-stained, warped license plate bolted to the trunk lid. Here's the breakdown of what actually matters.

What Makes Silicone the Better Choice

Rust — The Silent License Plate Killer

Metal license plate frames have one unavoidable weakness: they rust. Even "stainless" steel frames can develop surface rust after a winter of road salt exposure. The chrome-plated frames you see at every dealership are the worst offenders — once that chrome layer chips (and it will, from a single careless screwdriver slip), moisture gets underneath and the corrosion spreads invisibly behind your plate.

Silicone doesn't rust. Period. The Aujen Silicone License Plate Frame is made from industrial-grade silicone that's completely inert. It won't corrode, won't discolor, and won't leave rust stains on your actual license plate or your car's paint. For anyone living in a state with snow, rain, or coastal humidity, this alone is reason to switch.

The Rattle That Drives You Crazy

Every driver knows that annoying buzz coming from the rear of the car. Nine times out of ten, it's a loose metal license plate frame vibrating against the plate. The rigid metal-to-metal contact amplifies every bump and resonance frequency. Tightening the screws helps temporarily, but the vibration always comes back as the metal fatigues.

Silicone frames solve this by design. The flexible material naturally dampens vibration. The frame hugs the plate with a soft, grippy surface that doesn't transmit noise. You install it, tighten it once, and the rattle doesn't come back.

Water Trapping

Here's something most people don't think about: metal frames create a moisture trap. When water seeps between the metal frame and the plate, it has nowhere to go. That trapped moisture accelerates rust, damages the plate's reflective coating, and can even lead to your state's inspection sticker peeling off.

The Aujen silicone frame includes three drainage holes that allow water to escape. Combined with the silicone's natural water-shedding properties, your plate stays dry and readable — which is the whole point of having a license plate in the first place.

🚗 Pro tip: When installing any license plate frame, put a thin layer of dielectric grease or anti-seize compound on the screws. It prevents galvanic corrosion between the screw and frame, making future removal much easier — especially important with metal frames that tend to weld themselves to the screw over time.

When a Metal Frame Still Makes Sense

Metal frames aren't all bad. They come in a much wider variety of styles, colors, and finishes — chrome, brushed steel, black powder coat, even anodized aluminum. If you're building a specific aesthetic for your car (like a chrome-heavy classic car or a matte-black modern build), a metal frame might match your look better than silicone's single matte black option.

Metal frames are also typically cheaper upfront. You can find basic chrome frames for under $5 at auto parts stores. The trade-off is you'll likely replace them every 1–2 years when the corrosion becomes visible, making the total cost of ownership actually higher than a single silicone frame that lasts 5+ years.

The Bottom Line
